catalog_quote: Tonalità. A formola isolata delle voci costituite da varie radici, che in realtà non sono che voci semplici o monosillabiche, l'accento cade sull'ultima, mentre nel contesto del discorso può questa stessa voce o sillaba, assumere lo stesso rilievo delle altre. Così diventa poco pratico l'impiego di segni speciali di tonalità, e noi procureremo di adoperarli il meno possibile. [de Gregorio 1901: 145] ... 9. Der Wortton liegt meist auf der Endsilbe. 10. Gleichlautende Wörter werden mitunter durch die Intonation unterschieden. Wir unterscheiden dabei den steigenden und den fallenden Ton eines Vokals (ersterer durch á, letzterer durch à bezeichnet). [Seidel 1904: 40] ... Bei mehrsilbigen Wörtern hat die letzte Silbe in der Regel den Wortton. Die Satzbetonung ist, bis zum wichtigsten Worte in einer Steigerung begriffen, von da an fällt sie in einer Art von Cadenz. ... Man hat drei Tonstufen zu unterscheiden: Hochton, Tiefton und Tonlosigkeit. Aber der musikalische Ton ist sogar für die Bedeutung des einzelnen Wortes entscheidend: ein Wort, das in der Schrift unverändert bleibt, kann je nach der Tonhöhe, in der es gesprochen wird, verschiedene Bedeutung haben. [Henrici 1891: 18] ... Loanwords from French, where final stress is common, have been borrowed with final falling tone [Lotven 2020: 20] ... Le Gen a deux tonèmes HAUT et BAS qui sont des traits syllabiques oppositionnels. [Bolé-Richard 1983: 118, snippet]

new_statements.quote: Tonalità. A formola isolata delle voci costituite da varie radici, che in realtà non sono che voci semplici o monosillabiche, l'accento cade sull'ultima, mentre nel contesto del discorso può questa stessa voce o sillaba, assumere lo stesso rilievo delle altre. Così diventa poco pratico l'impiego di segni speciali di tonalità, e noi procureremo di adoperarli il meno possibile. [Concordant: Henrici 1891: 18 'Bei mehrsilbigen Wörtern hat die letzte Silbe in der Regel den Wortton.']
new_statements.translation: Tonality. In the isolated form of words made up of several roots -- which in reality are nothing but simple or monosyllabic words -- the accent falls on the last [syllable], whereas in connected discourse this same word or syllable may take on the same prominence as the others. Thus the use of special tonality marks becomes impractical, and we shall try to use them as little as possible. [Henrici 1891: 'In polysyllabic words the last syllable as a rule carries the word accent.']
new_statements.citation: de Gregorio, Giacomo. 1901. Sulla struttura della lingua evé (ewe, ephe, epe) in base a proprie raccolte dal vivo: osservazioni glottologiche. Studi glottologici italiani 2: 129-223.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again., p. 158 = printed p. 145 (running head 'LINGUA EVÉ. 145'), rendered and read: paragraph 'Tonalità. A formola isolata delle voci costituite da varie radici, che in realtà non sono che voci semplici o monosillabiche, l'accento cade sull'ultima, mentre nel contesto del discorso può questa stessa voce o sillaba, assumere lo stesso rilievo delle altre. Così diventa poco pratico l'impiego di segni speciali di tonalità, e noi procureremo di adoperarli il meno possibile.' -- verbatim as reported (also the scanned textof). It follows a 'Quantità' paragraph and precedes sec. 7 consonants, i.e. it is the whole of what de Gregorio says on prosody. Concordant Henrici 189…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation (isolated) forms of polysyllabic words, prominence ('accento'/'Wortton') is heard on the final syllable; in connected speech this final prominence is levelled. Both 1891/1901 observers otherwise recognise lexically distinctive pitch (Henrici: Hochton/Tiefton/Tonlosigkeit). Modern descriptions analyse Gen as a two-toneme (H/L) language (Bolé-Richard 1983: 118; Gblem-Poidi 2017: 15; Lotven 2020: H, L, marginal HL) and, as far as could be seen, say nothing about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: de Gregorio: in connected discourse the final syllable may have no more relief than the others. Henrici 1891: 104 notes demonstratives (ehe, esi, eke..) with 'Ton' on the first syllable; 'in der Regel' (as a rule) hedges the final-syllable rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms only; explicitly neutralised at phrase level per de Gregorio. Both statements are pre-tonological impressionistic observations (1891, 1901) that do not separate stress from lexical tone; Gen is a tone language and the modern primary description (Bolé-Richard 1983, seen only in snippets) lists tone as the sole oppositional prosodic feature of the syllable with no accent feature. Treat 'fixed: final syllable' as the historical observers' percept, not an established modern analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: de Gregorio 1901 is based on a native of Klein-Popo/Anecho (Aného) and states that Anecho is the variety principally studied (pp. 132, 142) = Gen genn1243 (Capo's Anexo dialect). Henrici 1891 covers 'Ephe' across three dialects -- Anlo (= Ewe, ewee1241), Anecho (= Gen, genn1243) and Dahome (= Fon, fonn1241) -- so his p. 18 rule is not Gen-specific. Lotven 2020 describes a speaker from Batonou, Togo (Gengbe). Westermann 1907 is Ewe proper (ewee1241), context only.

new_statements.quote: 9. Der Wortton liegt meist auf der Endsilbe. 10. Gleichlautende Wörter werden mitunter durch die Intonation unterschieden. Wir unterscheiden dabei den steigenden und den fallenden Ton eines Vokals (ersterer durch á, letzterer durch à bezeichnet). Vokale mit steigendem Ton sind so zu sprechen, daß man mit der gewöhnlichen Stimmhöhe einsetzt und dann (aber in einem Atem) nach oben abweicht, etwa so, wie wenn man auf einen Ruf mit der Frage „ja—a?" antwortet. Beim fallenden Ton setzt man etwas höher, als der gewöhnliche Sprachton ist, ein und läßt dann die Stimme sinken [...] (p. 40). So unterscheidet man z. B. mí (wir) von mì (ihr). [...] Ebenso unterscheiden sich z. B. egá (Häuptling) und egà (Geld) u. s. w. (p. 41)
new_statements.translation: 9. The word stress lies mostly on the final syllable. 10. Words that sound alike are sometimes distinguished by intonation. We distinguish here the rising and the falling tone of a vowel (the former marked by á, the latter by à). Vowels with rising tone are to be pronounced so that one starts at the ordinary pitch of the voice and then (but in one breath) deviates upward, roughly as when one answers a call with the question 'ja—a?'. For the falling tone one starts somewhat higher than the ordinary speaking pitch and then lets the voice sink [...] (p. 40). Thus one distinguishes e.g. mí (we) from mì (you pl.). [...] Likewise egá (chief) and egà (money) are distinguished, etc. (p. 41)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Gen has an empty rule; the existing statement (de Gregorio 1901, p. 145, Anecho informant) reads 'tone language with a stress statement' and says the accent falls on the last syllable of a word in isolation. Seidel 1904 says the same: word stress mostly final, and the language has lexical rising/falling tone distinguishing homophones. Same type and same placement; Seidel adds the explicit tonal minimal pairs (mí/mì, egá/egà) and the hedge 'meist'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress ('Wortton') falls mostly on the final syllable of the word ('meist' = mostly, no exceptions listed for Anecho). Separately, the language has lexical pitch distinctions ('Intonation': rising vs falling tone on a vowel) that distinguish otherwise identical words, shown with minimal pairs and musical notation. Seidel keeps the two apart: sec. 9 is stress placement, sec. 10 is tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed for the Anecho dialect beyond the hedge 'meist' (mostly). For comparison, the parallel Part I statement for Anlo-Ewe (sec. 7, printed p. 2, p. 10) says deviations from final stress are marked with an acute accent; no such remark is made for Anecho, where the acute is instead used for rising tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Seidel 1904 Part II (pp. 39-71) explicitly describes the Anecho dialect ('Grammatische Elemente des Anecho-Dialektes der Ewe-Sprache in Togo'), i.e. the Aneho / Petit-Popo variety = Gen/Mina (genn1243); his printed sources for it are Henrici 1891 (Anecho conversations), Prietze's ZAOS III article, Koebele's Klein-Popo primer 1895 and Walter 1900. Part I (pp. 1-38) describes Anlo-Ewe (ewee1241), not Gen; it carries a parallel statement at sec. 7, printed p. 2 (p. 10): 'Der Wortton liegt meist auf der Endsilbe; Abweichungen sind durch einen dem Vokal nachgesetzten Akut gekennzeichnet', which is about Anlo and was not used for the Gen reading.

tone_statements.citation: Lotven, Samson & Kelly Berkson. 2016. Consonant-tone interactions in Gengbe. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 139(4, Supplement): 2214. [Abstract, 171st Meeting of the Acoustical Society of America, Salt Lake City, May 2016.]
tone_statements.quote: To this end, we present an overview of its consonant, vowel, and tonal inventories. Of particular interest is the fact that its two register tones, (L)ow and (H)igh, show systematic phonological variation based on the voicing of onset consonants. ... This lowering is phonologized in many H tone contexts, resulting in a Rising tone in many (but not all) morphophonological environments. The distinction is phonetically present in low tone as well, where it perseverates across the entire vowel and results in a lower register L (by approx. 20 Hz).
tone_statements.locator: abstract (JASA 139(4_Supplement): 2214; text as delivered by Crossref)
tone_statements.summary: 2 register tones L, H; depressor (voiced obstruent) onsets -> H realised as Rising (phonologised LH) in many contexts, L realised in a lower register.

tone_statements.citation: Bole-Richard, Rémy. 1982. Étude phonologique de la langue « gen » [position d'une thèse d'École admise en 1976; directeur d'études Maurice Houis]. Annuaires de l'École pratique des hautes études, IVe section, Sciences historiques et philologiques 111(1) (Positions de thèses d'École de l'année 1978-1979 et positions de thèses de IIIe cycle): 62-64.
tone_statements.quote: Le système tonal du Gen est composé de 2 tonènes : haut et bas. Le tonème haut a une réalisation modulée montante lorsqu'il est porté par une syllabe à consonne initiale sonore non sonante. Si la tonalité est un trait oppositionnel inhérent à la syllabe, la modulation doit par contre être considérée comme un trait contrastif lié à la présence de certains phonèmes périphériques dans la syllabe. ... Mot phonologique : Il est défini par la présence nécessaire d'une syllabe centrale et celle, accessoire, d'une syllabe non centrale initiale, et en outre, par ses traits oppositionnels (schème tonal) et contrastifs (centralité, non-centralité).
tone_statements.translation: The tone system of Gen consists of 2 tonemes: high and low. The high toneme has a rising modulated realisation when carried by a syllable with a voiced non-sonorant initial consonant. While tonality is an oppositional feature inherent to the syllable, modulation must instead be regarded as a contrastive feature tied to the presence of certain peripheral phonemes in the syllable. ... Phonological word: it is defined by the necessary presence of a central syllable and the optional presence of an initial non-central syllable, and further by its oppositional features (tonal scheme) and contrastive features (centrality, non-centrality).
tone_statements.summary: 2 tonemes H, L; TBU syllable; H -> rising after voiced obstruent onset (depressor), modulation contrastive not tonemic; word-level tonal scheme.

tone_statements.citation: Prietze, Rudolf. 1897. Beiträge zur Erforschung von Sprache und Volksgeist in der Togo-Kolonie. Zeitschrift für afrikanische und oceanische Sprachen 3: 17-64. Berlin: Dietrich Reimer (Ernst Vohsen).
tone_statements.quote: Der emphatische Accent (stress, zerfallend in Haupt-, Nebenaccent und Unbetontheit) und der tonische (Hoch-, Mittel-, Tiefton) decken sich hier nicht derart wie im Deutschen; ... Im Uebrigen scheint, wie bereits oben bemerkt, im Ane̱ẖo-Dialekt die Intonation, d. h. die Unterscheidung von sonst gleichlautenden Stämmen nach der Tonhöhe, eine im Verhältniss zu den westlichen Nachbarn sehr untergeordnete Stelle zu spielen, soweit sich aus einer Vergleichung der hierdurch differenzirten Aṅlō-Worte bei S und H mit den betr. Ane̱ẖo-Stämmen ersehen liess. Ausser den erwähnten mu und wo begegneten mir bis jetzt nur sehr vereinzelte, nicht einmal ganz sichere Fälle.
tone_statements.translation: The emphatic accent (stress, divided into main accent, secondary accent and lack of stress) and the tonal accent (high, mid, low tone) do not coincide here the way they do in German; ... For the rest, as noted above, in the Anecho dialect intonation, i.e. the distinction of otherwise identical stems by pitch, seems to play a very subordinate role compared with the western neighbours, as far as could be seen from a comparison of the Anlo words so differentiated in S[chlegel] and H[enrici] with the corresponding Anecho stems. Apart from the mu and wo just mentioned I have so far met only very isolated, not even quite certain cases.
tone_statements.locator: p. 22 (last paragraph) and p. 23, Einleitung, section '3. Sprechweise und Betonung'; first announced p. 19
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Three pitch steps (Hoch/Mittel/Tiefton) recognised, grammatical H on neg. mu / 3pl wo, but lexical tone contrasts claimed marginal in Anecho vs Anlo (1897 outlier claim).

sources.note: Syllable prosodic features are oppositional (tonalité) vs contrastive (syllabicité, asyllabicité, modulation); 'Le système tonal du Gen est composé de 2 tonè[m]es: haut et bas'; the H toneme is realised as a rising modulation on a syllable with a voiced non-sonorant initial (depressor effect), so modulation is contrastive, not a third toneme; /b/-/m/ and /d/-/n/ provisionally kept distinct because they behave differently with respect to syllable tone (p. 63); the phonological word is defined by its 'schème tonal'; falling modulation, vowel sequence and vowel length act as demarcative signs be…

The high toneme has a rising modulated realisation when carried by a syllable with a voiced non-sonorant initial consonant. While tonality is an oppositional feature inherent to the syllable, modulation must instead be regarded as a contrastive feature tied to the presence of certain peripheral phonemes in the syllable. ... Phonological word: it is defined by the necessary presence of a central syllable and the optional presence of an initial non-central syllable, and further by its oppositional features (tonal scheme) and contrastive features (centrality, non-centrality).
tone.summary: 2 tonemes H, L; TBU syllable; H -> rising after voiced obstruent onset (depressor), modulation contrastive not tonemic; word-level tonal scheme.
tone.says: Syllable prosodic features are oppositional (tonalité) vs contrastive (syllabicité, asyllabicité, modulation); 'Le système tonal du Gen est composé de 2 tonè[m]es: haut et bas'; the H toneme is realised as a rising modulation on a syllable with a voiced non-sonorant initial (depressor effect), so modulation is contrastive, not a third toneme; /b/-/m/ and /d/-/n/ provisionally kept distinct because they behave differently with respect to syllable tone (p. 63); the phonological word is defined by…

tone.translation: The emphatic accent (stress, divided into main accent, secondary accent and lack of stress) and the tonal accent (high, mid, low tone) do not coincide here the way they do in German; ... For the rest, as noted above, in the Anecho dialect intonation, i.e. the distinction of otherwise identical stems by pitch, seems to play a very subordinate role compared with the western neighbours, as far as could be seen from a comparison of the Anlo words so differentiated in S[chlegel] and H[enrici] with the corresponding Anecho stems. Apart from the mu and wo just mentioned I have so far met only very isolated, not even quite certain cases.
